parole.significato: An ancient small boat made of wickerwork covered with a hide or leather.
parole.testo: From Latin carabus. The entomological sense is borrowed from translingual Carabus, from the same Latin source.

parole.significato: Having the form of a snake
parole.testo: From Latin coluber and translingual Coluber + -iform.

parole.significato: A climbing leguminous plant of Southeast Asia and the southwest Pacific Islands, Derris elliptica, whose roots are a so…
parole.testo: From New Latin and translingual Derris, from Ancient Greek δέρρις (dérrhis, “leather, skin”), referring to the leathery pods, from δέρω (dérō, “I skin, I flay”).

parole.significato: Relating to, or resembling, a gooseberry.
parole.testo: From New Latin grossularius, from translingual Grossularia, a subgenus of Ribes, including the gooseberry, from French groseille. The mineral name is in reference to a particular green variety found in Siberia.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Malus (the apples).
parole.testo: From Latin mālus and translingual Malus.

parole.significato: Any of the carnivorous mammals of the genus Mustela.
parole.testo: From Latin mūstēla and translingual Mustela.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a sparrow; sparrow-like; bird-like.
parole.testo: From Latin passer (“sparrow”), + -iform. Borrowed from translingual Passeriformes in the taxonomic sense.

parole.significato: Any of various succulent plants, of the genus Sedum, native to temperate zones; the stonecrop.
parole.testo: From Middle English cedum, from Latin sedum (“houseleek”). Modern usage is a semantic loan from translingual Sedum.

parole.significato: Any fossil ammonite of the genus †Turrilites, the shell forming an open spiral with the later whorls separate.
parole.testo: From Latin turris (“tower”) + -lite or directly from translingual †Turrilites.
